slides.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?

paragraphs.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?
Assessment of the Parcelbird Now proposal and recommendation to the board
Board meeting, January 2027
Prepared from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data); no external research

slides.title: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash

paragraphs.text: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash
Market
The market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it
US quick-commerce GMV grew 42% a year, 2022–25. Both incumbents lose money on every order (EBITDA margins −26% and −46%); QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities.
Economics
A Parcelbird dark store would lose money on every order, and customers don't stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost

Loss of $6.17 per order at benchmark median, and $1.76 with best-observed inputs on every driver. Only the founders' plan (+$2.02) is profitable, and it beats the best site ever observed on all four drivers. Our pop-up lost $12.57 per order; 22% of its customers were still ordering in month 3.
Funding
Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints
The launch needs $9.5M; only $7.2M can be spent while keeping 12 months of runway. Adding today's core burn, cash runs out in month 13. At benchmark economics, 9 stores would lose $18M a year.
Alternative
The software business is a better use of the same cash

It breaks even in about month 26 at today's 60% growth (month 36 at 40%) and never drops below 12 months of runway, provided growth stays at 34% or more. Selling store-based fast delivery to pipeline grocers gives Parcelbird a share of the market's growth.

Decisions for the board: (1) decline the 2027 launch and do not extend the pop-up; (2) approve the $0.8M a year of software hires, phased against signed contracts; (3) build a store-based fast-delivery offer for the grocers in the pipeline; (4) adopt explicit re-entry triggers, tracked through our customers' sites, before quick commerce is reconsidered.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

slides.title: We started from the founders' answer, "launch", and tested the six conditions it needs; the evidence supports none of them

paragraphs.text: We started from the founders' answer, "launch", and tested the six conditions it needs; the evidence supports none of them
Initial hypothesis tested: “Parcelbird should launch Parcelbird Now: 9 dark stores in 3 cities, contribution-positive per order by month 18.”

data: What would have to be true
1. The market has a profit pool, not just growth
GMV +42% a year, but contribution per order is −$1.90 (Zipcart) and −$3.40 (QuickBasket); QuickBasket shut 36% of its cities
2. A dark store makes money per order at achievable inputs
−$6.17 per order at benchmark median; −$1.76 even with every best-observed input combined
3. Parcelbird runs stores better than the benchmark
The pop-up was below the median on all four drivers (AOV, promotions, rider productivity, density)
4. Customers stay long enough to repay acquisition cost
$38 CAC; 22% still ordering in month 3; CAC is never repaid at benchmark or pop-up economics
5. The plan fits current cash with 12 months of runway
$9.5M needed vs $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; no new funding expected
6. It beats the best other use of the cash
The software business can reach break-even within current cash if growth stays at 34% or more

paragraphs.text: So what: the hypothesis fails on every condition, so we reverse it. The rest of the deck sets out the evidence in the order of the table.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

At benchmark-median inputs a Parcelbird store would lose $6.17 per order; $2.67 of that is lost before any site cost, so more volume cannot fix it
Contribution per order at benchmark median (14 customer sites, 2025), $
How to read it
Each order brings in $11.17 (goods margin plus delivery fee) and costs $13.84 in promotions, picking, riders and payment before the store's rent and staff are counted.
Why volume can't fix it
Higher density spreads the $3.50 of site cost over more orders, but each extra order still loses $2.67. The model only turns positive if AOV or rider productivity rise sharply.
Biggest cost line
Riders: $7.40 per order, 81% of the goods margin. Two of our three cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

Contribution per order by input scenario, $
No site has achieved the best-observed case
The best AOV ($42) and the best density (1,400 orders/day) come from different sites. Combining them is already optimistic, and it still loses money.
Nine stores at network scale
Median: −$18.2M a year. Best observed: −$8.1M a year. Founders' plan: +$11.9M a year. Only the plan's inputs give a profitable network.
Break-even AOV
With other inputs held, the median store needs an AOV of $63 and the best-observed store $50. The median is $34 and the best ever observed is $42.
Definition

"Before site fixed cost" covers the variable costs of each order. "After" also spreads each store's $1.15M a year of rent, staff and utilities (pop-up: $0.65M) across its orders. Both figures exclude HQ overhead, capex and marketing.

Sanity check on scale

9 stores × 1,800 orders × $45 × 365 days = $266M a year of sales in three mid-size cities. That is more than QuickBasket's total 2025 revenue ($210M) across all its cities, and about 5% of the entire 2025 US market ($5.1B).
(This compares our GMV with their reported revenue, which we take to be roughly equivalent for an operator that sells the goods itself.)

The plan is most exposed to AOV and rider productivity, the two drivers it stretches furthest. Falling short on density or promotions alone still leaves a thin positive margin of about $0.2–0.3 per order, but nothing for HQ overhead or marketing.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

slides.title: Our own Columbus pop-up came in below the benchmark median on every driver, so there is no evidence yet that we run stores better than others

paragraphs.text: 1 Market

Our own Columbus pop-up came in below the benchmark median on every driver, so there is no evidence yet that we run stores better than others
The founders' case for a capability edge

"Our software already runs other people's dark stores, so we know how to run them better than anyone." The pop-up is the only test of this, and it did worse than the median of the stores our software runs.
Fair caveat: it was early

Six weeks on a temporary site. Orders grew 18% a week, from roughly 179 a day in week 1 to roughly 408 in week 6 (our estimate from the compounding). But that growth came with 12% promotions and $38 of acquisition cost per customer.
Implication
Even if density reached the median, the store would still lose $6.17 per order (p. 5). Ramp-up alone does not close the gap.
Pop-up site cost: $650,000 a year ÷ (280 × 365 orders) = $6.36 per order. Rider cost: $17.75 ÷ 2.1 = $8.45 per order.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

slides.title: Zipcart's one profitable city needed a $3.99 fee and near-zero promotions, and it lost 14% of its volume; the same moves on our median store still lose $1.05 per order

paragraphs.text: 1 Market
2 Economics
3 Funding
4 Alternative
Zipcart's one profitable city needed a $3.99 fee and near-zero promotions, and it lost 14% of its volume; the same moves on our median store still lose $1.05 per order
Applying Zipcart's Q4 2025 moves to the benchmark-median store, contribution after site cost, $/order
What the investor update leaves out
"Zipcart turned contribution-positive (+$0.40 per order)" was true only for its densest city, after a new $3.99 fee on every order and a cut in promotions to 1%. Volume in that city then fell 14%.
What it would take for us

With those moves, a median store before site cost earns +$3.02 per order. To cover $1.15M of site cost it needs about 1,042 orders a day after the fee rise: 16% above today's median, 3.7× the pop-up, and with no loss of rider productivity at the lower volume.
Read-across
A profitable route may exist, but only at top-quartile density with premium pricing. This is not where a new entrant starts, and nothing in our data shows it yet.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

With software ARR still growing 60% a year, cash falls below 12 months of runway in month 5 and below zero in month 13 (model, p. 14).
Even if the $9.5M covered all company spending
$12.0M − $9.5M = $2.5M left at month 18: about 6 months of runway at today's burn, against the 12 required.
If benchmark economics apply rather than the plan's
A mature 9-store network loses about $18M a year ($1.5M a month), more than our total cash every year. The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator "unlikely".
The floor rises once stores are operating, because a higher burn needs a larger reserve to cover 12 months. The $7.2M of headroom is therefore a ceiling.

Software-first stays within current cash and the runway rule as long as ARR keeps growing at least 34% a year, just over half today's 60%
Software-first projected cash balance, $M, by annual ARR growth rate
Break-even ARR = opex ÷ 81% = $8.9M ÷ 0.81 = $11.0M, against $4.1M today.
The pipeline supports the hires: the 9 late-stage grocers are worth $0.86M of ARR; all 37 are worth $3.55M. The $0.8M of hires pays for itself with 10 contracts (28% of the pipeline).

What has to be true: 34% growth means about 15 net new contracts in year 1, and 60% means about 26. Costs must also stay flat apart from the hires. The pack does not give churn or win rates, so phase the hires against signed contracts.

slides.title: We ask the board to make four decisions in January 2027 and review progress in 90 days

paragraphs.text: We ask the board to make four decisions in January 2027 and review progress in 90 days

data: Decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now
Do not commit capex to dark stores and do not extend the pop-up (annualised loss about $1.3M). Keep the pop-up data and cohort learning.
2 engineers and 2 sales hires ($0.8M a year), released in two tranches tied to signed late-stage contracts (9 grocers, $0.86M ARR)
Package picking and rider dispatch for grocers who want fast delivery from existing stores; test it with late-stage pipeline accounts
Adopt re-entry triggers and runway reporting
Quarterly dashboard of the 4 triggers from customer-site data, plus monthly runway against the 12-month rule

paragraphs.text: 90-day checkpoint (April 2027): late-stage conversions against the 9 grocers, pilot interest in store-based fast delivery, actual ARR growth against the 34% minimum, and the first trigger dashboard. If growth is tracking below 34%, hold the second tranche of hires.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis
